title: Continuous Audit and Assurance
answer: Ledger anomaly detection, substantive testing, inventory observation, going concern analysis and controls testing.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Ledger Anomaly Detection
children.blurb: Ledger anomaly detection covers the review of journal entries, subledger transactions, reconciliations, master data changes and access events for patterns that depart from expected accounting behavior.

children.name: Substantive Testing at Full Coverage
children.blurb: Substantive testing at full coverage means applying audit procedures to every item in a defined population rather than to a sample.

children.name: Inventory Observation and Valuation
children.blurb: Inventory observation and valuation covers the evidence that inventory exists, is owned or controlled, is complete, is in saleable condition, and is carried at the right amount in the financial statements.

children.name: Going Concern Analysis
children.blurb: Going concern analysis in continuous audit and assurance is the ongoing evaluation of whether an entity can meet its obligations and continue operating for the foreseeable future.

children.name: Internal Control Testing
children.blurb: Internal control testing covers the design and operating effectiveness of controls that support reliable financial reporting, compliance and operations.

sections.body: Continuous audit and assurance is the use of software to watch a company's financial records as they change, rather than sampling them once a year. In practice, models scan every journal entry for patterns that look unusual, flag duplicate payments, odd posting times, or entries that reverse just before a reporting date. Auditors use these tools to test whole populations instead of a sample, so a test that once covered fifty invoices can now cover all of them. The same methods support inventory checks through image and sensor data, and they feed going concern work by tracking cash, covenants and supplier behaviour over time. The aim is not to replace the auditor's judgement but to point attention at the transactions that deserve it.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Anomaly detection works well on clean, high volume data and poorly where records are messy or the business is unusual, and it produces false positives that someone still has to clear. Full population substantive testing is technically feasible for many transaction types, though the quality of the conclusion depends on the quality of the underlying data and the model's calibration. Inventory observation has moved partly to drones, fixed cameras and computer vision, which count and locate stock but still struggle with condition, obsolescence and valuation judgement. Going concern analysis remains a judgement-heavy area where models can surface warning signals but cannot weigh management's plans or the reliability of a forecast. Internal control testing is the most mature use, since sampling and walkthroughs translate fairly directly into automated checks, yet no regulator has accepted a fully automated audit opinion. The honest limit across all five areas is that these systems assist evidence gathering and risk assessment, and a human remains accountable for the conclusion.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages follow the arc of an audit from raw records to the final opinion. Ledger Anomaly Detection is the entry point, covering how every entry gets scored and what makes a flag worth chasing. Substantive Testing at Full Coverage takes that flagged population and explains how whole-dataset testing replaces sampling, including where it still falls short. Inventory Observation and Valuation moves from numbers to physical assets, covering cameras, drones and the valuation judgements that vision systems cannot make. Going Concern Analysis sits later in the engagement, tracking the signals that bear on whether a business can continue, and it depends on the cash and transaction evidence built up in the earlier pages. Internal Control Testing closes the loop by examining the controls that produced the data in the first place, so a reader who wants to know whether the records can be trusted at all should start there and work back.
